facts.claim: Hamel Husain calls error analysis the most important activity in evals: it finds the failure modes unique to your application and data, and tells you which evals to write.
Open coding: a reviewer reads traces and writes open-ended notes on any issue they see, like a journal. The method is adapted from qualitative research.
Note the first failure you see in a trace: upstream errors can cause the problems that show up downstream.
Axial coding sorts the open notes into a failure taxonomy, then counts the failures in each category. Hamel Husain calls it the most important step.
A working pool of roughly 100 diverse traces is a useful guide; keep reviewing until new traces stop revealing new failure modes.
Annotate at least 30 traces yourself before you review an AI agent’s suggested notes.
A domain expert, someone who knows what a good answer looks like, should do the reviewing.
Error analysis keeps your eval metrics grounded in what the application really does, instead of generic metrics that don’t help.

OpenTelemetry, an open standard for recording traces, keeps shared names for the spans, metrics and events of model calls, agents and tools. Its span names are still marked Development, not yet stable.
In those conventions every span carries gen_ai.operation.name; its well-known values include invoke_agent, retrieval, chat and execute_tool, and a tool span names its tool in gen_ai.tool.name.
Zhang et al. (2025) marked the step that decided each failure in the failed runs of 127 AI agent systems; the best automatic method found that step only 14.2% of the time.
Shankar et al. (2024) found that people need criteria to grade a model’s outputs, but grading outputs is what helps them define the criteria. They call it criteria drift.

Cemri et al. (2025) had expert reviewers read 150 traces of multi-agent AI systems and sort the failures into 14 modes in 3 groups; the reviewers agreed closely (a kappa of 0.88, where 1 is full agreement).
NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023) measures risk by two things together: how much harm an event would do, and how likely it is to happen.
Chen, Zaharia and Zou (2023) found the same model service can change within months: GPT-4 told prime from non-prime numbers 84% of the time in its March 2023 version, 51% in June.
Guest, Bunce and Johnson (2006) coded 60 interviews and found no new themes after the first 12; the basic ones were there by the sixth.
